name: Sega Master System
description: Sega's 8-bit console, released in Japan as the Mark III in 1985 and redesigned as the Master System for the West. It lost badly to the NES in Japan and North America but did well in Europe and especially Brazil, where Tectoy kept making it for decades.

specs.sound: SN76489 PSG in VDP; YM2413 FM on JP model

curiosities: In Japan it was the Mark III, launched on 20 October 1985 for ¥15,000.
Sega of America staff picked the name Master System by throwing darts at a whiteboard of ideas.
It had a slot for credit-card-sized Sega Card games as well as cartridges.
A Sega Card held up to 32 KB; a cartridge up to 512 KB.
In 1987 Sega handed US sales to the toy maker Tonka, which had never sold a video game; Sega took them back in 1989.
The US launch bundle came with Hang-On and Safari Hunt on one cartridge.
The Light Phaser was modelled on the gun from the anime Zillion.
The SegaScope 3-D Glasses used LCD shutters to create a stereoscopic image.
The Master System II dropped the card slot, so it couldn't use the 3-D Glasses.
To cut costs, the Master System II also lost the reset button, power light, expansion port and start-up music.
Later models had games such as Alex Kidd in Miracle World built in.
Only the Japanese model had the Yamaha YM2413 FM sound chip built in.
Its Z80A is rated for 4 MHz but runs at 3.58 MHz.
It shows up to 32 colours at once, out of 64.
In 1990 it was Europe's best-selling console; in the UK it outsold Nintendo's 150,000 to 80,000.
In Australia it sold 250,000 in 1990 alone, beating the NES.
In Brazil, Tectoy claimed 80% of the market; Nintendo only arrived there officially in 1993.
Samsung sold it in South Korea as the Gam*Boy from April 1989.
Tectoy's Master System 3 Collection (2006) has 120 games built in.
The Game Gear, code-named Project Mercury, was built on Master System hardware.
story: Sega's SG-1000 had lost to the Famicom, so it built the Mark III in 1985, then restyled it as the Master System for the West in 1986.

It was technically stronger than the NES but Nintendo's licensing kept most publishers away, and in North America it struggled. In Europe, and above all in Brazil, where Tectoy built and sold it for decades, it was a great success. Alex Kidd, Phantasy Star, Wonder Boy III and the 8-bit Sonic games were its stars.
Its hardware lived on almost unchanged in the Game Gear, and Tectoy still sells Master Systems with games built in.
